title: The poem and its occasion
short: Written on 2 November 1883 for an art auction raising money for the Statue of Liberty's pedestal; inscribed on a plaque inside the pedestal in 1903.
body: Bartholdi's statue, 'Liberty Enlightening the World', was a gift from France, but the pedestal had to be paid for by Americans, and in 1883 a fund-raising Art Loan Exhibition was organised in New York. William Maxwell Evarts and Constance Cary Harrison asked Emma Lazarus (1849-1887) for a contribution; she wrote the sonnet on 2 November 1883. It was largely forgotten at the statue's unveiling in 1886. After her death her friend Georgina Schuyler campaigned to commemorate it, and in 1903 a bronze plaque with the poem was fixed inside the pedestal. The poem largely created the statue's later meaning as a welcome to immigrants, rather than the Franco-American celebration of republican liberty its makers intended.

title: the brazen giant
short: The Colossus of Rhodes, a huge bronze statue of the sun-god Helios (c. 280 BC), one of the Seven Wonders, famous in legend for straddling the harbour.
body: The Colossus of Rhodes, made by Chares of Lindos to celebrate the city's survival of a siege, stood about 33 metres high and fell in an earthquake some sixty years later; Pliny the Elder describes its fallen fragments (Natural History 34.41). 'Brazen' means made of brass or bronze, and also, by a pun, shameless or impudent. The image of a giant 'astride from land to land', legs planted on either side of the harbour, is a medieval and Renaissance legend, not ancient fact, familiar from Cassius's 'he doth bestride the narrow world / Like a Colossus' (Julius Caesar 1.2). Lazarus sets the conquering male colossus against her new female one.

title: sea-washed, sunset gates
short: The entrance to New York harbour; 'sunset' because America is the land of the setting sun, the West, to those arriving from Europe.
body: The 'gates' are the harbour entrance through which ships reached New York. 'Sunset' marks America as the West, the direction of the setting sun for European voyagers, a long-standing figure in which the New World is the Hesperides or westward land of promise. The gates are 'sea-washed' because they open on the Atlantic. The phrase is answered in the last line by 'the golden door': gates of arrival framing the sonnet.

sources.cite: Museum of the City of New York, 'The New Colossus'

anchor: A mighty woman with a torch
title: a mighty woman with a torch
short: The statue's female figure holding up a torch; Lazarus makes the torch a lamp of welcome, not of conquest.
body: Bartholdi's statue personifies Liberty as a robed classical woman holding a torch aloft, a tablet in her other hand. Lazarus, writing before the statue was erected, stresses gender: the Rhodian Colossus is a 'giant' with 'conquering limbs'; the new colossus is a 'mighty woman', and her power is used to welcome, not to dominate. The torch reappears as the 'lamp' of the final line, moving from a symbol of enlightenment to a domestic lamp held at a door.

sources.cite: National Park Service, Statue of Liberty National Monument, 'Emma Lazarus'

title: imprisoned lightning
short: Electricity: the torch was to be lit electrically, so its flame is lightning harnessed and confined.
body: The phrase is a modern conceit: the statue's torch was to be illuminated by electric light, the new technology of the 1880s (Edison's Pearl Street station opened in New York in 1882). Lightning 'imprisoned' is natural force tamed, an image of American ingenuity. There may also be a glance at Franklin, the American who identified lightning with electricity. Lazarus's 'imprisoned' quietly sets up a paradox in a poem about freedom: the light of liberty is itself captive.

sources.cite: Museum of the City of New York, 'The New Colossus'

title: Mother of Exiles
short: Lazarus renames the statue: not 'Liberty Enlightening the World' but a mother receiving the displaced, especially the Jewish refugees she worked with.
body: The official name of Bartholdi's statue was 'Liberty Enlightening the World'. Lazarus substitutes a maternal title. The choice reflects her own work from 1881 with Jewish refugees fleeing the Russian pogroms, many of whom were housed on Ward's Island in New York; she wrote and campaigned on their behalf and became an advocate for a Jewish homeland. 'Exiles' recalls the biblical exile of Israel. Esther Schor's biography stresses how the poem joins Lazarus's Jewish advocacy to a vision of America as refuge.

title: twin cities
short: New York and Brooklyn, separate cities until 1898, which faced each other across the harbour.
body: In 1883 Brooklyn was an independent city, the third largest in the United States; it was consolidated with New York only in 1898. The harbour lies between them. 'Air-bridged' suggests the harbour 'bridged' by the air above it, or more specifically the Brooklyn Bridge, opened in May 1883, six months before the poem was written, the first bridge to link the two cities. Not all commentators accept the bridge reference, but the date makes it likely.

sources.cite: Museum of the City of New York, 'The New Colossus'

title: Petrarchan sonnet and volta
short: A Petrarchan sonnet (abbaabba cdcdcd); at the volta the statue speaks, and description becomes direct speech.
body: The octave describes the statue and rejects the ancient colossus; the sestet gives her silent speech. The rhyme scheme is strict Italian (fame/stand/land/flame ... she/poor/free), and the turn at l. 9 is marked by quotation marks. The paradox 'cries she / With silent lips' acknowledges that the statue cannot literally speak; the poet speaks for her. The choice of the Petrarchan sonnet, an Old World form, for a New World manifesto is itself a kind of transplanting.

title: storied pomp
short: The celebrated grandeur and history of the Old World, 'storied' meaning famous in story; perhaps echoing Gray's 'storied urn' and 'pomp of power'.
body: 'Storied' means celebrated in history or legend, and also decorated with scenes from history (as a storied window or urn). Lazarus's statue tells Europe to keep its monuments and aristocratic splendour; America asks instead for the poor. The phrasing recalls Gray's Elegy, where 'the pomp of pow'r' leads but to the grave and no 'storied urn' can recall the dead (ll. 33-41). Gray's poem, which honours the obscure poor against the proud, is an apt subtext for a sonnet that honours the 'wretched refuse'.

sources.cite: Thomas Gray, 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard' (1751), ll. 33-41

title: huddled masses
short: Crowded together for warmth or safety, as steerage passengers were; the phrase has become proverbial.
body: 'Huddled' gives the image of people pressed together, cold and frightened, the conditions of steerage passengers on emigrant ships. 'Masses' was a political word of the period for the working poor. The line's famous phrase has been quoted and contested in American immigration debates ever since; in 2019 a federal official proposed rewording it, provoking controversy. In the poem, the masses are 'yearning to be free', the one place in the sestet where 'liberty' (the statue's real name) is directly invoked.

sources.cite: National Park Service, Statue of Liberty National Monument, 'Emma Lazarus'

title: wretched refuse
short: 'Refuse' means what has been rejected or thrown away; the Old World's rejected people are welcomed by the New.
body: 'Refuse' (stressed on the first syllable) is waste matter, what has been discarded; the word comes from Old French refus, 'refusal', and so means literally 'the refused'. It is a deliberately harsh word: Europe treats its poor as rubbish, and the statue takes them in. Some readers have found it condescending to the immigrants; others read it as Lazarus's bitter irony against Europe's view of them. 'Wretched' (miserable, also in the old sense 'exiled', Old English wrecca) and 'teeming' (overcrowded) intensify the picture.

title: tempest-tost
short: Tossed by storms at sea; a phrase with biblical and Shakespearean precedent (Isaiah 54:11; Macbeth 1.3).
body: The emigrant crossing of the Atlantic was dangerous, and the homeless are pictured as storm-tossed sailors arriving in port. The phrase has strong literary ancestry: in Isaiah 54:11 God comforts Zion, 'O thou afflicted, tossed with tempest, and not comforted', promising to rebuild her; and in Macbeth one of the witches curses a sailor whose 'bark cannot be lost, / Yet it shall be tempest-tost' (1.3). The Isaiah passage, addressed to exiled Israel and promising restoration, fits Lazarus's Jewish concerns especially well.

sources.cite: The Holy Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Isaiah 54:11

title: I lift my lamp
short: The torch becomes a lamp, the domestic light held up at a door to guide the traveller home.
body: The torch of l. 4 is now a 'lamp', a homelier word: the statue is less a beacon of enlightenment than a woman at the door of her house, holding up a light for those arriving at night. Lamps in scripture are images of guidance ('Thy word is a lamp unto my feet', Psalm 119:105), and the wise virgins' lamps await the bridegroom (Matthew 25). The alliteration on l binds the closing line.

sources.cite: The Holy Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Psalm 119:105

title: the golden door
short: The entrance to America, golden with promise and sunset light; it closes the sonnet's frame of gates and doors.
body: The 'golden door' answers the 'sunset gates' of l. 3: the harbour entrance is now the door of a house, golden with the light of the lamp and of the setting sun, and with the promise of prosperity ('streets paved with gold' was a byword among emigrants). The image completes the poem's transformation of a colossal monument into a hospitable home. Within a decade the federal immigration station on Ellis Island (opened 1892) would become the literal door, and the poem's line is now associated with it.
